concepts.title: L, a, b Color Space Blurring Sensitivity
concepts.one_liner: The human eye is sensitive to blurring in the luminance component of the L, a, b color space but relatively insensitive to blurring in the chromatic components.
concepts.content:
In a red-green-blue (RGB) representation, the eye is sensitive to high spatial frequency changes in both red and green. A rotation of the color coordinates of the image, followed by a nonlinear stretching, can put the image into a color space called L, a, b. In that space, the eye is very sensitive to any blurring of the L color component, called luminance, but is relatively insensitive to blurring of the a or b components. This effect is commonly exploited in image compression, allowing some image components to be sampled more coarsely than others.

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) RGB components. (c) RGB components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls2)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls1 (b) and @fig-girls1 (c). (a) R component blurred, G and B components sharp. (b) G component blurred, R and B components...)

(see figure: (a) Original image. (b) Lab components. (c) Lab components, each blurred. These sharp and blurred components are used in the color images of @fig-girls4)

(see figure: Color images composed of sharp and blurred components from figures @fig-girls3 (b) and @fig-girls3 (c). Fig (a) L component blurred, a and b components sharp. (b) a component blurred, L and b...)
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding human visual perception allows for more efficient image compression. By identifying which color components (like luminance) the eye is sensitive to and which (like the a and b channels) it is not, we can selectively reduce data quality in insensitive areas without noticeably degrading the image.
concepts.recap_md: - The L, a, b color space separates luminance (L) from chromatic components (a and b).

concepts.title: Color Gamut
concepts.one_liner: The gamut is the range of colors that a system can represent or reproduce.
concepts.content: The gamut is the range of colors available to a system. Some input colors may fall outside this range if they require negative values to be represented.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the gamut is essential for determining which real-world colors can be accurately reproduced by a specific display or printing technology.
concepts.recap_md: - The gamut represents the total range of reproducible colors.

slots.motivation: Understanding the gamut is essential for determining which real-world colors can be accurately reproduced by a specific display or printing technology.

concepts.title: Conditions for Perfect Color Reproduction
concepts.one_liner: Perfect color reproduction requires the system's sensitivity functions to be a linear combination of the eye's photoreceptor sensitivities.
concepts.motivation_md: To ensure that a reproduction system mimics human vision, its sensors must respond to light in a way that is mathematically consistent with the eye's own spectral sensitivities.
concepts.recap_md: - Color matching requires system sensitivities $\mathbf{C}$ to be a linear combination of eye sensitivities $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$.

slots.motivation: To ensure that a reproduction system mimics human vision, its sensors must respond to light in a way that is mathematically consistent with the eye's own spectral sensitivities.

concepts.title: Example Color Matching System
concepts.one_liner: A valid color matching system is defined by spectral sensitivity curves and corresponding primary lights.
concepts.content:
A valid color matching system is defined by the elements of two matrices, $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{P}$. For a color reproduction system to be physically realizable, the elements of the primary spectra, $\mathbf{P}$, must be non-negative.

[FIGURE:77907696848a7f82 | A graph showing three color matching functions, $\bar{r}(\lambda)$, $\bar{g}(\lambda)$, and $\bar{b}(\lambda)$, plotted against wavelength $\lambda$ in nanometers from 400 to 700. The blue curve...]

[FIGURE:fec594ff8e0f61e8 | A plot showing three narrow vertical spikes representing primary light spectra on a wavelength axis from 400 to 750 nm. A blue spike is located near 440 nm, a green spike near 540 nm, and a red spike...]

The elements of the matrices $\mathbf{C}$ and $\mathbf{P}$ for an example color matching system include: (a) Spectral sensitivity curves, the rows of a color measurement matrix, $\mathbf{C}$. These should be linear combinations of the eye's photosensitivity curves, $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$. (b) Corresponding primary lights, $\mathbf{P}$, satisfying $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{P}= \mathbf{I}_3$ (where $\mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_3$).
concepts.motivation_md: This example demonstrates how theoretical color matching conditions are applied to physical systems using specific sensitivity curves and primary light sources.
concepts.recap_md: - Primary spectra $\mathbf{P}$ must be non-negative to be physically realizable.

concepts.title: CIE XYZ Color Space
concepts.one_liner: The CIE XYZ color space is a standard defined by all-positive color matching functions.
concepts.content:
A color space is defined by the matrix $\mathbf{C}$, which contains three rows of color sensitivity functions. These functions must be a linear combination of the eye's sensitivity functions, $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$. One color standard is the Commission Internationale de l'Eclairage (CIE) *XYZ* color space, $C_{\mbox{CIE}}$. The CIE color matching functions, which are the rows of $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{CIE}}$, were designed to be all-positive at every wavelength.

(see figure: CIE color matching functions @cie1931)
concepts.motivation_md: Standardizing color spaces like CIE XYZ allows for consistent color communication and measurement across different devices and industries.
concepts.recap_md: - The CIE XYZ color space uses sensitivity functions that are linear combinations of human eye sensitivities.

concepts.title: CIE Color Matching Functions
concepts.one_liner: CIE color matching functions are all-positive spectral sensitivity curves used to define the CIE XYZ color space.
concepts.content:
The CIE color matching functions, represented as the rows of the matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{CIE}}$, were designed to be all-positive at every wavelength.

concepts.motivation_md: By designing these functions to be all-positive, the CIE created a system where any visible color can be represented with positive coordinates, simplifying calculations.

concepts.title: Tristimulus Values
concepts.one_liner: Tristimulus values $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are coordinates found by projecting an input spectrum onto CIE color-matching functions.
concepts.content: To find the CIE color coordinates, one projects the input spectrum onto the three color-matching functions. This process yields coordinates called tristimulus values, which are labeled $X$, $Y$, and $Z$.
concepts.motivation_md: Tristimulus values provide a numerical way to describe how a complex light spectrum will be perceived by the human eye.
concepts.recap_md: - Tristimulus values $X$, $Y$, and $Z$ are the coordinates in the CIE color space.

slots.motivation: Tristimulus values provide a numerical way to describe how a complex light spectrum will be perceived by the human eye.

slots.example: To find the CIE color coordinates, one projects the input spectrum onto the three color-matching functions. This process yields coordinates called tristimulus values, which are labeled $X$, $Y$, and $Z$.

concepts.title: CIE Chromaticity Coordinates
concepts.one_liner: CIE chromaticity coordinates $x$ and $y$ represent color normalized by the sum of the tristimulus values.
concepts.content: **CIE chromaticity coordinates** are defined as $x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}$ and $y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}$.
concepts.motivation_md: Chromaticity coordinates allow for the description of color (hue and saturation) independently of its luminance (brightness).
concepts.recap_md: - $x = \frac{X}{X+Y+Z}$ and $y = \frac{Y}{X+Y+Z}$.

concepts.title: Spatial Resolution and Color Sensitivity
concepts.one_liner: Human spatial resolution varies across different directions in color space, a fact exploited in image compression.
concepts.content:
Color interacts with our perception of spatial resolution. The eye is very sensitive to fine spatial modulations in some directions in color space, while it is relatively insensitive in others. Some color coordinate systems take advantage of this disparity to enable efficient representation of images by sampling image data sparsely along color axes where human perception is insensitive to blurring.

As expected from the spatially varying pattern of color sensors in the eye—specifically the scarcity of blue or short-wavelength sensors—humans observe different colors with different spatial resolutions. This fact is exploited in image compression methods.
concepts.motivation_md: By understanding that the human eye is less sensitive to detail in certain color channels (like blue), engineers can compress images more effectively by discarding information the eye wouldn't notice anyway.
concepts.recap_md: - Human spatial resolution is different for different colors due to the distribution of sensors in the eye.

concepts.title: Visible Light Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The visible light spectrum is the narrow band of electromagnetic wavelengths, approximately 400 nm to 700 nm, that the human eye can perceive as color.
concepts.content: Light is a mixture of electromagnetic waves of different wavelengths. Sunlight has a broad distribution of light of the visible wavelengths. At an air/glass interface, light bends in a wavelength-dependent manner; a prism disperses the different wavelength components of sunlight into different angles, and we see different wavelengths of light as different colors. Our eyes are sensitive to only a narrow band of that electromagnetic spectrum, the visible light, from approximately 400 nm to 700 nm, which appears blue to deep red, respectively.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the visible spectrum is fundamental to optics and color science, explaining how white light is composed of various wavelengths that our visual system interprets as distinct colors.
concepts.recap_md: - Visible light ranges from approximately 400 nm (blue) to 700 nm (red).

slots.motivation: Understanding the visible spectrum is fundamental to optics and color science, explaining how white light is composed of various wavelengths that our visual system interprets as distinct colors.

concepts.title: Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: The term spectrum refers to the decomposition of white light into its constituent colors.
concepts.content: Newton understood that white light could be decomposed into different colors and invented the term spectrum.
concepts.motivation_md: The concept of a spectrum allows us to categorize and analyze light based on its component colors or wavelengths rather than treating it as a single monolithic entity.
concepts.recap_md: - The spectrum is the array of colors produced when white light is decomposed.

concepts.title: Refraction
concepts.one_liner: Refraction is the bending of light at a material boundary, which varies by wavelength to separate white light into colors.
concepts.content: The bending of light at a material boundary is called refraction, and its wavelength dependence lets the prism separate white light into its component colors.
concepts.motivation_md: Refraction is the physical mechanism behind lenses and prisms, enabling the manipulation of light paths and the separation of light into its spectral components.
concepts.recap_md: - Refraction occurs when light changes direction while passing from one medium to another.

concepts.title: Diffraction
concepts.one_liner: Diffraction is the separation of light into spectral components through the constructive interference of scattered light in different directions.
concepts.content:
Diffraction is a way to separate light into its spectral components, where constructive interference of scattered light occurs in different directions for different wavelengths of light. 

A simple spectrograph can reveal the spectrum of light based on diffraction from a compact disk (CD). Light passes through a slit and strikes the CD tracks. Constructive interference from the light waves striking the tracks occurs at a different angle for each wavelength, yielding a separation of the different wavelengths of light according to their angle of diffraction.

concepts.motivation_md: Diffraction provides an alternative to refraction for spectral analysis, allowing for the creation of gratings and spectrometers that can precisely measure the wavelength composition of light.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffraction uses wave interference to separate light by wavelength.

concepts.title: Fovea
concepts.one_liner: The fovea is a region of the eye where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.content: The fovea is a region of the eye characterized by a specific sampling pattern where there are no rods and the cones are close-packed.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the fovea is essential for modeling how the eye samples light at its highest resolution, as the absence of rods and dense packing of cones define our central vision.
concepts.recap_md: The fovea contains no rods.

concepts.title: Cone Response Matrix Equation
concepts.one_liner: Photoreceptor responses can be described using matrix algebra as the product of a spectral sensitivity matrix and an incident light vector.
concepts.content: We can describe the photoreceptor responses using matrix algebra. If the matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$ consists of the spectral sensitivities of the L, M, and S cones in three rows, and the vector $\mathbf{t}$ is a column vector of the spectrum of light incident on the eye, then the L, M, and S cone responses will be the product: $$\begin{bmatrix} L \\ M \\ S \\ \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}} \, \mathbf{t}$$
concepts.motivation_md: This matrix representation allows for a computationally efficient way to predict how the human eye will respond to any given light spectrum.
concepts.recap_md: - The matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$ contains spectral sensitivities for L, M, and S cones.

slots.motivation: This matrix representation allows for a computationally efficient way to predict how the human eye will respond to any given light spectrum.
slots.key_passage: - The matrix $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$ contains spectral sensitivities for L, M, and S cones.

concepts.title: Color Matching Principles
concepts.one_liner: Color matching is the process of adjusting primary colors to reproduce a target color, based on the principle that any color appearance can be matched by a linear combination of three primaries.
concepts.content: Color science provides methods to analyze and reproduce color, allowing image displays to match target colors and ensuring consistency in manufactured items and food standards. (see figure: The USDA color standards for French fried potatoes, one of many color standards @Munsell2020) A key task is predicting when two colors will be perceived as a match, such as adjusting a display to match a reflecting surface. Despite different spectra, colors can almost always be made to match. This performance is inferred from the spectral sensitivity curves of receptors. Experimentation shows that any color appearance can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors, due to the three classes of photoreceptors in the eye. These matches are transitive: if color A and color B both match the same combination of primaries, they match each other. The amounts of each primary required serve as coordinates for the color.
concepts.motivation_md: Color matching is the foundation of the color industry, enabling the consistent reproduction of colors across different media, from digital displays to physical products like food and branded materials.
concepts.recap_md: - Any color can be matched by a linear combination of three primary colors.

concepts.title: Primary Colors
concepts.one_liner: Primary colors are reference colors whose linear combination can match the appearance of any other color.
concepts.content: Primary colors are reference colors used to match a target color. Through experimentation, it has been discovered that the appearance of any color can be matched through a linear combination of three primary colors. This phenomenon is a direct result of the presence of three classes of photoreceptors in human eyes. These color matches are transitive; if color A matches a specific combination of primaries and color B matches that same combination, then color A will match color B. Consequently, the amount of each primary required to match a color can serve as a set of coordinates indicating that color.
concepts.motivation_md: Primary colors exist because humans have three types of cone cells; they provide a basis for representing the entire gamut of human color perception using only three variables.
concepts.recap_md: - Any color appearance can be matched by a linear combination of three primary colors.

concepts.title: Color Metamerism
concepts.one_liner: Color metamerism occurs when two different light spectra appear to be the same color because they produce the same response in the eye's photoreceptors.
concepts.content: Two different spectra are metameric if they appear to be the same color to our eyes. There is a large space of metamers: any two vectors describing light power spectra that give the same projection onto a set of color matching functions will look the same. While light spectra exist in a high-dimensional space, human vision only perceives projections onto a 3D subspace.
concepts.motivation_md: Metamerism is what makes color reproduction possible; we don't need to replicate the exact physical spectrum of an object to make it look the same to a human observer.
concepts.recap_md: - Metamers are different light spectra that are perceived as the same color.

slots.motivation: Metamerism is what makes color reproduction possible; we don't need to replicate the exact physical spectrum of an object to make it look the same to a human observer.
slots.key_passage: - Metamers are different light spectra that are perceived as the same color.

concepts.title: Color Reproduction System
concepts.one_liner: A color reproduction system is defined by three spectral sensitivity curves that are linear combinations of the eye's spectral sensitivities.
concepts.content: A color reproduction system is defined by first specifying its three spectral sensitivity curves. These are organized into a $3 \times N$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, where $N$ is the number of spectral samples over the visible range. The three curves should be a linear combination of the eye's spectral sensitivity curves, or $\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \, \mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}}$, where $\mathbf{R}$ is any full-rank $3 \times 3$ matrix. This allows translation between different color spaces by applying a $3 \times 3$ matrix transformation to change basis vectors, which do not need to be orthogonal. (see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...)
concepts.motivation_md: This framework allows engineers to design cameras and displays that accurately capture and recreate colors by ensuring the system's sensors relate mathematically to human visual sensitivities.

These are organized into a $3 \times N$ matrix, $\mathbf{C}$, where $N$ is the number of spectral samples over the visible range. This allows translation between different color spaces by applying a $3 \times 3$ matrix transformation to change basis vectors, which do not need to be orthogonal. concepts.title: Derivation of Color Matching Conditions
concepts.one_liner: The derivation of color matching conditions identifies the relationship between primary lights, sensor sensitivities, and mixing matrices required for perfect color reproduction.
concepts.content: (see figure: A color reproduction system. Light sensors a, b, and c respond to the input light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$, giving sensor activations $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. Combinations of those activations drive the...) For a given set of primary lights $\mathbf{P}$, we seek a matrix of color sensitivity curves $\mathbf{C}$ and a $3 \times 3$ matrix $\mathbf{M}$ to allow perfect color reproduction. The eye's response to a light spectrum $\mathbf{t}$ is $\mathbf{C}_{\mbox{eye}} \mathbf{t}$. In a reproduction system, sensors produce $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$, which are mixed by $\mathbf{M}$ to control primaries $\mathbf{P}$, resulting in an output spectrum $\mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t}$. For perfect reproduction, the eye's response to this output must match its response to the original: $\mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{t}$. Since this must hold for any $\mathbf{t}$, the condition is $\mathbf{C}_{eye} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}_{eye}$. By requiring the sensor subspace $\mathbf{C}$ to be a linear combination of the eye's subspace ($\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R} \mathbf{C}_{eye}$), we derive the condition $\mathbf{C} \mathbf{P} \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{I}_3$, where $\mathbf{I}_3$ is the identity matrix.
concepts.motivation_md: This derivation provides the mathematical constraints necessary to ensure that a camera-display system produces colors that are perceptually identical to the original scene.
concepts.recap_md: - Perfect reproduction requires the eye's response to the output spectrum to match its response to the input.

concepts.title: Primary Lights
concepts.one_liner: Primary lights are a set of three lights whose combination can be controlled to match the eye's response to a given light spectrum.
concepts.content: A color reproduction system measures an input light and produces an output light that matches the color appearance of the input. A camera with a screen display is an example, where colors in the world are measured and then reproduced. We can match the eye's response to a given light spectrum through the appropriate control of a sum of three lights, called the primary lights. In a display screen, the three color elements of each pixel serve as the primary lights.
concepts.motivation_md: Primary lights are the physical components (like LED subpixels) that allow electronic devices to generate a wide range of perceived colors by stimulating the eye's three cone types in specific proportions.
concepts.recap_md: - Primary lights are the physical light sources used to reproduce colors in a system.

concepts.title: Color Appearance of Different Spectral Bands
concepts.one_liner: The visible spectrum can be divided into three 100 nm bands—blue, green, and red—whose combinations determine the approximate color appearance of light.
concepts.content: The visible spectrum lies roughly in the range between 400 and 700 nm. We can divide the visible spectrum into three 100 nm bands and study the appearance of light power spectra where power is present or absent from each of those three bands. (see figure: The approximate color appearance of light over different spectral regions.) Light with spectral power distributed in just the 400–500 nm wavelength band will look some shade of blue, while light in the 500–600 nm band will appear greenish. Most distributions within the 600–700 nm band will look red. White light is a mixture of all spectral colors; a spectrum containing power evenly distributed over 400–700 nm would appear approximately white. Light with no power in any of those three bands, that is, darkness, appears black. There are three other spectral classes in this simplified grouping: spectral power present in two bands but missing in the third. Cyan is a combination of blue and green (roughly 400–600 nm), sometimes called minus red. Magenta is a combination of blue and red (400–500 nm and 600–700 nm), or minus green. Red and green together (500–700 nm) make yellow, or minus blue. (see figure: For coarse orientation only, this cartoon model gives the color appearance of different spectral bands of the spectrum of visible light.)
concepts.motivation_md: Developing a feel for how different spectral bands contribute to perceived color helps simplify the complex relationship between physical light spectra and subjective human vision.
concepts.recap_md: - The visible spectrum (400–700 nm) can be simplified into three primary bands: blue, green, and red.

concepts.title: Diffuse Surface Reflection Model
concepts.one_liner: The diffuse reflection model describes the reflected power spectrum as the wavelength-by-wavelength product of incident light and a surface's reflectance spectrum.
concepts.content: When light reflects off a surface, the power spectrum alters in ways that depend on the surface's characteristics and geometry. While reflections can be complex and described by the bidirectional reflectance distribution function (BRDF), many matte reflections are characterized by a diffuse reflection model. In this model, the power spectrum of the reflected light, $r(\lambda)$, is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the power spectrum of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and a reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of the surface: $$r(\lambda) = k \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) s(\lambda),$$ where the proportionality constant $k$ depends on the reflection geometry. This wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is also a good model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through an attenuating filter, where the incident power spectrum is multiplied by a transmittance spectrum. (see figure: Reflectance spectra from two flowers @Arnold2010. The blue *Hepatica nobilis* flower @nobilis and the orange flower, *Pyrostegia venusta* @venusta}.)
concepts.motivation_md: Modeling how surfaces modify light spectra is essential for understanding how we perceive object colors and for simulating realistic light-surface interactions in computer graphics.
concepts.recap_md: - Diffuse reflection is modeled as the product of the incident light spectrum and the surface's reflectance spectrum at each wavelength.

concepts.title: Reflectance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: A reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ represents the proportion of incident light a surface reflects at each wavelength.
concepts.content: The reflectance spectrum, $s(\lambda)$, of a surface is used to determine the reflected light spectrum. In the diffuse reflection model, the reflected power spectrum is proportional to the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the incident light, $\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, and this reflectance spectrum.
concepts.motivation_md: It provides a physical description of a material's color properties independent of the light source illuminating it.
concepts.recap_md: - The reflectance spectrum $s(\lambda)$ defines a surface's intrinsic color characteristics.

concepts.title: Transmittance Spectrum
concepts.one_liner: A transmittance spectrum describes the wavelength-by-wavelength scaling of light as it passes through an attenuating filter.
concepts.content: The transmittance spectrum of an attenuating filter describes how the incident power spectrum is multiplied at each wavelength as light passes through it. This wavelength-by-wavelength scaling is a model for the spectral changes to light caused by transmission through such a filter.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding transmittance is crucial for designing filters and understanding how transparent or translucent materials alter the color of light.
concepts.recap_md: - Transmittance spectra characterize how filters or materials attenuate light at different wavelengths.

concepts.title: Color Constancy and Illumination Estimation
concepts.one_liner: Color constancy is the visual system's ability to estimate surface reflectance by accounting for the unknown spectrum of the illumination.
concepts.content: To estimate surface colors, a vision system must estimate the illumination spectrum and the surface reflectance spectra from observations of only their products. When the illumination is white light, the observed reflected spectrum is proportional to the reflectance spectrum of the material. However, under unknown illumination, a visual system must estimate the surface reflectance spectrum by taking the context of nearby image information into account. Algorithms to do this range from simple heuristics to statistical and neural network approaches. Humans do not solve this perfectly, as seen in the viral optical illusion of "The Dress." (see figure: A photograph of a striped dress that became a famous viral optical illusion. The dress features horizontal bands of lace and fabric that appear to some as blue and black, and to others as white and...) (see figure: A diagram illustrating the color constancy ambiguity of 'The Dress'. A central image of a striped dress is shown twice: once on the left under yellow 'warm illumination' where it appears as blue and...) The perceived colors of the dress depend on the assumed color of the illumination. Assuming warm, yellowish illumination leads to a perception of blue and black material, while assuming cool, blueish illumination leads to a perception of white and gold.
concepts.motivation_md: Color constancy allows organisms to recognize objects consistently across different lighting conditions, such as direct sunlight versus shade.
concepts.recap_md: - Color constancy involves disentangling the contribution of the light source from the intrinsic reflectance of a surface.

concepts.title: The Machinery of the Eye
concepts.one_liner: The human eye reduces the high-dimensional light spectrum into a three-dimensional description using three classes of cone photoreceptors.
concepts.content: While instruments like spectrographs can measure light power at hundreds of wavelengths, the human visual system obtains a useful description of the world from a much lower dimensional representation. The retina contains photoreceptors called rods and cones. Rods are used in low-light levels, while cones are used in color vision. The human visual system analyzes the incident light power spectrum with only three different classes of photoreceptors, called the L, M, and S cones because they sample at the long, medium, and short wavelengths. This gives the visual system a three-dimensional (3D) description of light, with each photoreceptor class taking a different weighted average of the incident light power spectrum. (see figure: A diagram showing a mosaic of red, green, and blue circles representing the spatial distribution of L, M, and S cones in a human retina. The red and green circles are most numerous and are arranged...) (see figure: A graph showing the normalized spectral sensitivity curves for the three types of human cone cells: S (short-wavelength, blue curve), M (medium-wavelength, green curve), and L (long-wavelength, red...) In the retina, cones are close-packed in a hexagonal pattern, particularly near the fovea, with a stochastic assignment of classes. Notably, the spatial sampling of S cones is much sparser than that of L or M cones.
concepts.motivation_md: Understanding the biological constraints of the eye explains why we perceive color the way we do and provides the basis for three-component color models like RGB.
concepts.recap_md: - Human color vision is trichromatic, based on three types of cone cells (L, M, and S).

concepts.title: Rods and Cones
concepts.one_liner: Rods and cones are the two types of photoreceptors in the retina, responsible for low-light vision and color vision, respectively.
concepts.content: The retina contains photoreceptors called rods and cones. Rods are used in low-light levels, and the cones are used in color vision. In low-light, only the rods operate and our vision becomes black and white.
concepts.motivation_md: This dual-receptor system allows the eye to function across a vast range of light intensities, from dim starlight to bright sunlight.
concepts.recap_md: - Rods provide high sensitivity for vision in low-light environments but do not perceive color.

concepts.title: L, M, and S Cones
concepts.one_liner: L, M, and S cones are the three classes of photoreceptors that sample long, medium, and short wavelengths to enable trichromatic color vision.
concepts.content: The human visual system analyzes the incident light power spectrum with three classes of photoreceptors: the L, M, and S cones, which sample long, medium, and short wavelengths respectively. This results in a three-dimensional (3D) description of light, where each class takes a different weighted average of the spectrum. (see figure: A diagram showing a mosaic of red, green, and blue circles representing the spatial distribution of L, M, and S cones in a human retina. The red and green circles are most numerous and are arranged...) (see figure: A graph showing the normalized spectral sensitivity curves for the three types of human cone cells: S (short-wavelength, blue curve), M (medium-wavelength, green curve), and L (long-wavelength, red...) These cones are arranged in a hexagonal packing in the retina, with L and M cones being much more numerous than the sparser S cones. This sampling pattern is most dense near the fovea.
concepts.motivation_md: These specific receptors define the spectral sensitivity of human vision and determine which wavelengths of light we can distinguish as different colors.
concepts.recap_md: - L, M, and S cones respond to long, medium, and short wavelengths, respectively.

prereq.rationale: The visible light spectrum is a specific subset of the general physical phenomenon of a spectrum.
Categorizing spectral bands into blue, green, and red requires the context of the 400-700 nm visible range.
The model is defined as the wavelength-by-wavelength product of the incident and reflected light power spectra.
The reflectance spectrum is a fundamental component of the diffuse reflection equation.
Color constancy is the computational task of recovering the reflectance spectrum from the product described in the diffuse reflection model.
The text explicitly links spatial resolution differences to the distribution of color sensors (cones), particularly the scarcity of blue sensors.
The phenomenon is explained as a direct consequence of the physical anatomy and sensor arrangement within the human eye.
The transformation to L, a, b space is described as starting from an RGB representation.
The human visual system is described as a mechanism that reduces the high-dimensional light power spectrum into a lower-dimensional representation.
L, M, and S cones are the three specific classes of cone photoreceptors used for trichromatic color vision.
The fovea is defined by its specific density and arrangement of rods and cones.
The matrix equation calculates the specific responses of the L, M, and S cones.
The ability to match colors with three primaries is a direct consequence of having three cone classes.
Primary colors are the reference colors used in the linear combinations that define color matching.
Metamerism occurs when different spectra result in the same cone response vector projection.
Reproduction systems are designed to relate their sensor sensitivities to the eye's cone responses.
Primary lights are the physical implementation of primary colors in a reproduction system.
The gamut is the set of all colors that can be formed by non-negative combinations of the primary lights.
The derivation provides the mathematical requirements for a reproduction system to achieve perfect matching.
The conditions are the formal mathematical results derived for perfect color reproduction.
The CIE XYZ space is a standard color space defined using the linear combination conditions for matching.
The CIE color matching functions are the specific sensitivity curves that define the XYZ space.
Tristimulus values are the coordinates obtained by projecting a spectrum onto the CIE matching functions.
Chromaticity coordinates are a normalized representation of the tristimulus values.

overlay.rationale: Refraction in a prism is a primary physical mechanism used to demonstrate the decomposition of light into a spectrum.
Diffraction provides an alternative physical mechanism to refraction for separating light into its spectral components.
The power spectrum provides a quantitative mathematical definition (intensity as a function of wavelength) for the qualitative concept of a spectrum.
The mapping of spectral bands to colors demonstrates how the distribution of power across wavelengths determines perceived color.
Both are functions of wavelength, but the power spectrum represents absolute intensity while the reflectance spectrum represents a ratio of reflected to incident light.
Transmittance describes light passing through a medium, whereas reflectance describes light bouncing off a surface; both use wavelength-dependent scaling.
The L, a, b space is a specific application of the principle that human vision has different spatial resolutions for different color components.
L, a, b is a perceptually-based color space often used in conjunction with CIE standards to represent color information.
The matrix equation provides a formal mathematical description of how the eye's machinery processes light.
The example provides concrete spectral curves and lights that satisfy the matching conditions.
